links.note: Why it is 5:30 pm in India when it is noon in London - this concept states that Indian Standard Time is 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of the local time at Greenwich, which is the fact the answer turns on.

Why symbols and colours are needed on a map - this concept explains that there would not be enough space to draw every building, so a symbol represents each kind of feature and numerous details fit into the limited space.

Finding what lies in the eight directions from your home or school - this concept gives the four cardinal and four intermediate directions and closes with the same exercise, asking in which cardinal direction your home lies from your school.

Delhi and Bengaluru sharing a longitude of 77E and therefore the same local time despite different latitudes - the answer comes from this concept's rule that local time changes with longitude at 15 degrees to the hour, and latitude does not enter it.

Whether the Equator is also a parallel of latitude - this concept states that the Equator is the largest of the circles drawn parallel to it, so it is itself a parallel. Already linked and correct. Note: the printed answer belongs to a different statement in the same true-or-false set.

The crossword clue for a line across which the day and date change is the International Date Line, which this concept defines and places at approximately 180 degrees longitude. Already linked and correct.

Visiting a city for the first time and wanting to find places - this concept opens on exactly that situation, asking a local person or looking at a map of the city, and concludes that this is where a map comes in handy.
A map defined as a representation or drawing of some area, looked at as if viewing the surface from the top - this concept's definition, word for word.
An atlas as a book or collection of maps - defined in this concept beside the definition of a map.
A political map as the one showing countries or states, boundaries and cities - this concept names the three kinds of map, physical, political and thematic, which are the options.
The scale as the component that lets a huge place fit on a small piece of paper - this concept asks that question and answers it with the scale.
Reading 3 cm off a map at 1 cm = 500 m as 1500 m is a direct application of this concept's scale statement, where each centimetre represents a certain distance on the ground.
Why the scale must be known before measuring - this concept ends on the point that the actual distance between two points depends on the scale the map is using.
North, south, east and west as the cardinal directions or cardinal points - this concept's own naming. Already linked and correct.
Northeast, southeast, southwest and northwest as the intermediate directions - this concept names them in those words. Already linked and correct.
Most maps simply carrying an arrow marked with the letter N, pointing north - this concept's closing remark on direction.
The Survey of India, a government body, having fixed the set of symbols used for maps of India - this concept's sentence. Already linked and correct.
Pairing a map feature with the symbol that stands for it - this concept is the symbols component, where roads, railway lines, rivers and ponds each get a fixed symbol from the standard set.
The Earth nearly having the shape of a sphere, slightly flattened at the poles, which is what makes a flat representation impossible - this concept's opening.
The orange peel that cannot be flattened without tearing at the edges - this concept's own demonstration that a sphere cannot be laid flat. Already linked and correct.
Travelling from the bank on the city map - this concept's activity asks which way you would go to proceed from the bank to the market, on the same Fig. 1.1 the question uses.

The chessboard notation d2 to d4 marking a square by a letter and a number - this concept builds the idea of a pair of coordinates from the chessboard and the market shop before any geography is involved.
The Equator as the line halfway between the North and South Poles - this concept places it there while building latitude on the rotating globe.
Latitude as the measure of distance from the Equator towards a pole, expressed in degrees - this concept's definition. Already linked and correct.
The Equator as the largest of the circles drawn parallel to it, with the circles growing smaller towards the poles - this concept's statement.
The Equator taken by convention as latitude 0 degrees - this concept's convention. Already linked and correct.
The latitudes of the two poles being 90 degrees North and 90 degrees South, noted 90N and 90S - this concept states both.
The climate around the Equator being generally hot, also called torrid - this concept's link between latitude and climate. Already linked and correct.
The climate becoming more moderate or temperate as latitude increases away from the Equator - this concept's middle step. Already linked and correct.
The climate closer to the poles growing colder, or frigid - the last step of this concept's latitude-and-climate sequence. Already linked and correct.
Meridians of longitude as half-circles running from one pole to the other - this concept's definition, and its explicit contrast with the full circles of latitude. Already linked and correct.
Latitude and longitude together being the two coordinates of a place, with which any place on Earth can be located - this concept's statement.
India's north-south extent read off parallels of latitude - this is the chapter's latitude concept, where parallels and their degree values are defined. Already linked and defensible, so left alone.
India's west-east extent read off meridians of longitude - this is the chapter's meridian concept. Already linked and defensible, so left alone.
Crossing the International Date Line eastward and subtracting a day, from Monday to Sunday - this concept's rule. Already linked and correct.
Why the Date Line deviates from the 180 degree meridian, to avoid dividing some countries into two different days - this concept explains its own hedge. Already linked and correct.

Spotting the title as the option that is not a map component - two of the three real components, direction shown by the north arrow and symbols standing for real features, are defined in this concept, which is where the chapter's list of components closes.
